After spearheading the alt-country movement with Uncle Tupelo, Jay Farrar pursued his vision with Son Volt, who recorded three landmark albums in the ’90s before the groundbreaking artist put the band on extended hiatus and cut three solo LPs. Missing the free exchange of ideas and the surprises that inevitably occur when a group of simpatico musicians lock together, Farrar assembled a new lineup of Son Volt in 2004 and has since released nine albums. The latest album, Sound Signal Serenades, was released as a special 2026 Record Store Day limited edition LP. Jay Farrar’s work often seeks out the ghosts of America’s discordant or forgotten past, converses at length with them, and writes songs that stake a claim to a better future.

item.title: Visitor's Center to Folk Art Center — Mon Sep 14, 9:00 AM
item.description:
Asheville Mountains-to-Sea Trail Hiking Club 2.0 This is an easy to moderate hike, and we have a pace of about 30 to 3.2 mph. We take the Visitor's Center Loop to the Mountains to Sea Trail and turn around at the Folk Art Center. This hike is slightly over 5 miles. We should return between 11 and 11:10. There's is only one climb and it's on the way back, up some steps and a hill near Gashes Creek.
Mountains-to-Sea-Trail hikes are designed for fitness and community among people who are already reasonably fit. It's not an endurance hike by any means, but it is designed so we can get our hearts beating a bit while still being able to have a conversation and meet new people. We stop at the 1/2 way point for a few minutes.

item.title: Appalachian Flooding in Fact and Fiction — Wed Sep 16, 5:30 PM
item.description:
In “Appalachian Flooding in Fact and Fiction,” Nico Zegre, Ph.D., explores how floods work, what flooding looks like in Appalachia, and why floods are changing. He will discuss how the region’s steep topography, narrow valleys, and limited flat land for development contribute to significant flood risks, as well as how flooding connects Appalachian communities through space and time. Literary scholar Jessica Cory, Ph.D., examines representations of flooding in Appalachian literature, from early works to contemporary depictions in twenty-first-century texts, including the recent anthologies Had I a Dove: Appalachian Poets on the Helene Flood, edited by Hilda Downer, and Troublesome Rising: A Thousand-Year Flood in Eastern Kentucky, edited by Melissa Helton. Through mapping literary floods across the region, Cory explores how water connects us, even in disastrous ways. This event is free and open to the public; however, registration is encouraged. item.description:

Usually fewer than 20 percent of those attending are members of HPC. About Jennifer Sperry Steinorth Jennifer Sperry Steinorth’s books include “Boys Behind Glass,” “Her Read: A Graphic Poem,” and “A Wake with Nine Shades.” She is a finalist for the Eric Hoffer Prize, a recipient of the Foreword Reviews Bronze Prize for Poetry, and a recipient of the Fred Whitehead Award from the Texas Institute of Letters. item.title: Lea and Heffernan of Wheelchair Sports Camp — Fri Oct 9, 3:00 PM
item.description:
Gaelynn Lea and Kalyn Rose Heffernan of Wheelchair Sports Camp will visit UNC Asheville for an afternoon talk and evening performance. At 3 p.m., Lea and Heffernan will discuss disability culture, access, and activism, sharing their experiences as artists and advocates working to make the arts more inclusive. At 6 p.m., Wheelchair Sports Camp will take the stage for a free performance. Lea, winner of NPR Music’s Tiny Desk Contest, is an accomplished violinist, songwriter, composer, and disability advocate who has performed around the world and composed the score for Macbeth on Broadway. Wheelchair Sports Camp, led by wheelchair-using rapper Kalyn Rose Heffernan, blends hip-hop, humor, and high-energy performance. The Denver-based band has expanded its work beyond music into performance art, museums, theater, film, and activism. Both events are free and open to the public and will take place in the Blue Ridge Room of the Highsmith Student Union.
